common_name: Atropurpureum Japanese Maple (Classic Red-Leaf Seedling Maple)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Atropurpureum is the classic old red-leaf Japanese maple selection from which many later-named red cultivars were derived.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Atropurpureum is the classic old red-leaf Japanese maple selection, first distributed from Dutch nurseries in the mid-1800s, from which many later-named red cultivars were selected as chance seedlings. Because it is propagated from seed as well as by grafting, plants sold as Atropurpureum vary somewhat in leaf color intensity and habit, but typically show reddish-purple, deeply five- to seven-lobed leaves in spring that fade to a bronzed green through summer heat — a trait that distinguishes it from later, more color-stable selections like Bloodgood. It forms an upright, rounded small tree with reddish new twigs and clusters of small red-winged samaras in late spring that add additional color. Fall color is a good orange-red. In zone 8, afternoon shade and consistent moisture help prevent summer leaf scorch and premature color fade. Long grown as an understock and garden tree, Atropurpureum remains valued for its historic pedigree and reliable performance as a general-purpose red-leaf landscape maple.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Oshio Beni Japanese Maple (Orange-Red Spring Upright Maple)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full morning sun; Oshio Beni is a vigorous, heat- and sun-tolerant selection valued for reliable orange-red spring color.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full morning sun; Oshio Beni is a vigorous, heat- and sun-tolerant upright Japanese maple long popular in West Coast nursery production for its reliable orange-red spring color. New leaves emerge bright orange-red in spring, mature to a bronzed green through summer, and turn brilliant orange to red again in fall for a striking bookend display. Its strong, upright-spreading branching habit and above-average vigor make it a dependable landscape tree that tolerates more sun and heat than many red-leaf selections without significant scorch. Provide consistent moisture during hot weather and full morning sun with light afternoon protection in the hottest climates. Oshio Beni is widely used as an understock and landscape tree throughout USDA zones 5 through 8.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Suminagashi Japanese Maple (Deep Purple Marbled-Leaf Maple)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Suminagashi is an old cultivar with deeply cut, richly colored purple-red foliage on a vigorous upright-rounded tree.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Suminagashi is an old Japanese cultivar whose name, meaning 'floating ink,' references the traditional marbled-paper technique and alludes to the rich, saturated purple-red of its foliage. Unlike the finely dissected laceleaf types, its seven-lobed leaves are deeply and sharply cut but not fully dissected, giving a refined, lacy-textured look on a full-size upright-rounded tree. The dark reddish-purple color holds well into summer before shifting toward bronze-green, with good crimson fall color. A vigorous, easy-to-grow selection, Suminagashi performs reliably as a specimen or shade-garden tree given moist, well-drained soil and protection from the hottest afternoon sun.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Koto-no-ito's narrow, thread-like leaves are more wind- and scorch-resistant than broader-leaved cultivars.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Koto-no-ito is a distinctive narrow-leaf (linearilobum-type) Japanese maple cultivar whose long, slender, thread-like green lobes give the foliage an airy, almost willow-like texture quite unlike the classic star-shaped Japanese maple leaf. The narrow leaf form is naturally more resistant to wind tatter and scorch than broad-leaved or finely dissected cultivars, allowing it to tolerate more open, breezy sites. It forms a slow-growing, upright-arching small tree or large shrub, turning attractive gold to orange in fall. Its Award of Garden Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society reflects reliable garden performance. Site in moist, well-drained soil with some shelter from the hottest afternoon sun.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Skeeter's Broom Japanese Maple (Dense Columnar Red Maple)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Skeeter's Broom's dense, slow, columnar habit suits small gardens and container culture.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Skeeter's Broom is a dense, slow-growing upright cultivar selected for its tightly columnar habit and deep purple-red leaf color that holds unusually late into the season before other red cultivars begin to fade. Its compact, congested branching and modest ultimate size make it well suited to small gardens, narrow side yards, and large containers where a strongly upright accent is wanted without the eventual bulk of full-size red maples. New growth emerges rich burgundy-red and deepens further through the season, with good red fall color. Provide consistent moisture and afternoon shade in hot climates to preserve leaf color and prevent scorch.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Garnet Japanese Maple (Weeping Red Lace-Leaf Maple)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Garnet holds its rich red dissectum foliage color better through summer heat than many weeping red cultivars.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Garnet is a weeping, mounding lace-leaf Japanese maple selected for foliage color that holds its rich garnet-red better through summer heat than many red dissectum cultivars, which often fade toward bronze-green. The finely and deeply dissected leaves cascade over a broad, mounded, umbrella-like framework of arching branches, turning bright orange-red in fall. Its Award of Garden Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society reflects outstanding and reliable performance. As with other weeping laceleaf types, provide shelter from strong wind and hot afternoon sun, and keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched; Garnet is well suited to a prominent spot near a patio, pond, or garden entrance where its cascading form and color can be appreciated up close.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Beni Maiko Japanese Maple (Heat-Tolerant Scarlet Spring Maple)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Beni Maiko offers Shindeshojo-like scarlet spring color with notably better heat and sun tolerance.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Beni Maiko is a compact upright cultivar prized for brilliant scarlet-red new spring growth similar in intensity to Shindeshojo, but with notably better heat and sun tolerance, making it a popular and dependable choice in warmer nursery production regions. The bright red spring leaves mature to green or bronze-green through summer before turning red-orange again in fall. Its moderate size and dense, twiggy habit suit smaller gardens and container culture as well as mixed borders. Provide consistent moisture through summer heat and some afternoon shade in the hottest climates to keep the spring color show at its brightest.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Higasayama's cream, pink, and green variegated leaves are best sited with protection from the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Higasayama is an old variegated Japanese maple cultivar grown for its cream, pink, and green mottled foliage and for the distinctive rough, corky texture that develops on its bark with age — a striking bark feature shared by only a handful of Japanese maple cultivars. The upright, vase-shaped tree bears leaves irregularly splashed and margined with cream and pink over green, giving a bright, variegated presence through the growing season, with orange fall color. Variegation is generally best with some protection from the hottest midday and afternoon sun, which can scorch the pale leaf portions; dappled shade and consistent soil moisture keep the foliage looking its best through summer.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Vitifolium's large, vine-shaped leaves and exceptional fall color make it a long-prized full moon maple selection.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Vitifolium is an old English selection of the full moon maple, first distributed in the 1860s and named for its large, soft, vine-leaf-shaped (grape-leaf-like) foliage, distinctly larger and more coarsely lobed than typical Acer japonicum leaves. It tolerates somewhat more sun than most full moon maple cultivars and develops into a substantial large shrub or small tree with a graceful, spreading crown. Fall color is exceptional even by Japanese maple standards, with leaves turning through vivid combinations of orange, red, and purple, often on the same leaf, earning it long-standing recognition including the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Provide dappled shade, shelter from strong wind, and consistent summer moisture for best performance.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)

common_name: Moonrise Full Moon Maple (Coral Bark Shirasawanum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Moonrise pairs coral-red winter bark with gold-orange full moon maple foliage for year-round color.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Moonrise is a patented coral bark selection of the full moon maple, combining bright coral-red young stems that glow through the winter garden with gold-orange foliage color through the growing season — pairing the coral bark trait more familiar from Acer palmatum 'Sango-kaku' with the rounder, star-shaped leaves and slower, more compact growth habit typical of Acer shirasawanum. New spring leaves emerge orange-tinged before settling into gold, with good orange-red fall color that again highlights the colorful bark. Its upright, slow-growing habit suits smaller gardens and prominent winter-viewing locations near a patio or entry. Provide dappled shade and shelter from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, both of which scorch the gold foliage.

common_name: Wilson's Pink Dwarf Japanese Maple (Dwarf Mounding Pink-Tipped Maple)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Wilson's Pink Dwarf's small dense-mound scale suits rock gardens, troughs, and containers.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Wilson's Pink Dwarf is a slow-growing dwarf cultivar forming a dense, tightly congested mound of small leaves, with new spring growth emerging pink-tinged before maturing to green through summer and turning gold to orange in fall. Its very compact, twiggy habit and diminutive ultimate size make it one of the more useful truly dwarf Japanese maples for rock gardens, trough and container culture, and the front of small borders, and it has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for garden performance. Keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, and provide some afternoon shade in hot climates to protect the fine foliage from scorch.
sources: J.D. Vertrees & Peter Gregory, Japanese Maples (Timber Press)
